name: FDA and EMA Good AI Practice Principles
blurb: The ten principles the FDA and EMA agreed for AI across the medicine lifecycle.
title: FDA and EMA Good AI Practice Principles
answer: In January 2026 the FDA and EMA published ten shared principles for good AI practice in drug development, covering research, manufacturing and pharmacovigilance. They are high level: human centred design, a risk based approach, data quality, clear documentation, lifecycle monitoring and clear, essential information for users. They signal that both agencies will judge AI by the same basic tests.

reading.body:
In January 2026 the FDA and EMA published ten shared principles for good AI practice in drug development, covering research, manufacturing and pharmacovigilance.

The principles are deliberately high level. Human centred design, a risk based approach, data quality, clear documentation, lifecycle monitoring and clear information for users are the kind of tests that apply to any AI system, not just to medicine. What makes them notable is that two regulators with separate regimes agreed on the same list. A company building one governance policy around these ten items is building something that reads to both agencies, which is cheaper than maintaining two.

The principles are guiding principles, not regulations. They do not replace the FDA credibility framework or the EMA reflection paper, they sit above them. So the practical effect is on how submissions and inspections are assessed, not on what is legally required. A team that treats the ten principles as a checklist for its AI governance policy is aligning with how both agencies say they will judge AI, and that alignment is the whole of the benefit the data supports.

What the data does not cover is enforcement. There is no penalty attached here, no deadline, and no statement of how either agency will weigh a policy that maps to some principles and not others. It also says nothing about compute, data centre capacity or power, so nothing here should be read as a constraint on AI scaling. The constraint this data describes is regulatory attention, and it is a soft one.

terms.line: The field of computer science dedicated to creating systems that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence: understanding language, recognizing patterns, making decisions.
The documented pre-AI measurement of a metric, cycle time, error rate, cost, capacity, against which any AI improvement claim is tested. No baseline, no provable improvement, only impressions.

The subset of AI focused on systems that learn from data and improve with experience rather than following explicitly programmed rules. Nearly everything called AI in production is machine learning underneath.
The 2026 package of targeted amendments to the EU AI Act, deferring high-risk deadlines and restructuring conformity assessment.

The requirement that a person can understand, intervene in, and override AI decisions. Mandated for high-risk uses under the EU AI Act, and only real when the human has the time, information, and authority to actually intervene.
The policies, roles, and oversight processes an organization applies to its AI use: who may deploy what, under which controls, with what accountability.

explainer:
The principles were written to apply across the medicine lifecycle and to both agencies' oversight, so they read as a shared vocabulary rather than detailed rules. They ask that AI be designed around the people who use and are affected by it, that its use be justified by a risk based assessment, and that the data used to build and test it be relevant, representative and well governed.

They also expect clear documentation of how a model was built and validated, performance assessment suited to the context of use, monitoring through the whole lifecycle so that drift is caught, and plain, essential information for users about what the system does and its limits. For companies the value is practical: a governance policy organised around the ten principles maps cleanly onto both FDA and EMA expectations, which reduces the work of operating in both markets.

Where the principles came from

The FDA, Health Canada and the UK's MHRA jointly published guiding principles for good machine learning practice in medical devices, and have since added principles for transparency and for predetermined change control. The European Medicines Agency and the FDA have each set out principles for AI in medicine development and regulatory decision making. The documents differ in detail but describe the same core of good practice, which is why companies treat them together as the baseline.

The shared core

Multi disciplinary expertise across the model's life, so that clinical, engineering and regulatory judgement are all applied. Good software engineering and security practice. Training data that represents the intended patient population, with test data kept separate. Performance measured against a clinically relevant reference and across subgroups. A model designed for the data it will actually see and the people who will use it. Human factors and human oversight considered in the design. Clear communication to users of what the model does and its limits. And monitoring of deployed models with management of retraining risks.

How to use them

These principles are not a checklist that earns approval, but they are what reviewers and inspectors have in mind. The practical use is to map each AI product or process to them and write down the evidence for each, so that gaps are visible before a regulator finds them. Companies that do this report that most gaps are in documentation and monitoring rather than in the models, and that fixing them is a matter of discipline rather than research.
